Nor is there any cause for indignation against Hippo, who made his own death immortal; this Hippo ordered to be inscribed upon his monument this elegy: "This is the tomb of Hippo, whom Fate made equal to the immortal gods in his death." Well done, Hippo, you show us human error! For if they did not believe you while you spoke, let them become disciples of the dead man. This is an oracle of Hippo: let us mark it. Those whom you worship were once men, and then died; and myth and time have honoured them. For somehow the things present are wont, through familiarity, to be despised, while the things past, removed by the obscurity of time from immediate refutation, are honoured by fiction, and the one are disbelieved, the other admired. At any rate, the ancient dead, dignified by the long lapse of error, are reckoned gods by those that come after. Your pledge of these things is your very mysteries, your festivals, the bonds and wounds and weeping gods: "Ah, woe is me, that Sarpedon, dearest of men, is doomed to be slain by Patroclus son of Menoetius." The will of Zeus has been overcome, and Zeus laments for you over Sarpedon, defeated. Reasonably, then, have you yourselves called them idols and demons, since Homer too, honouring even Athena herself and the rest of the gods with wickedness, styled them demons: "And she went to Olympus, to the house of aegis-bearing Zeus, among the other demons." How, then, are the idols and the demons still gods, being in truth abominable and unclean spirits, admitted by all to be earthly and foul, weighed downward, lurking about the tombs and the monuments, where dim shadowy phantoms appear faintly? These are your gods, the idols, the shadows, and besides these those lame and wrinkled ones, "with eyes asquint," the Prayers, daughters rather of Thersites than of Zeus; so that it seems to me Bion said wittily, how could men justly ask of Zeus fair offspring, which he could not even provide for himself? Alas for the godlessness! The incorruptible essence — as far as in you lies — you bury, and that pure and holy being you have heaped into the tombs, robbing the truly existing essence of its divinity. Why, then, have you assigned to the things that are not gods the prerogatives of God? Why, forsaking heaven, have you honoured earth? What else is gold, or silver, or adamant, or iron, or bronze, or ivory, or precious stones? Are they not earth, and from earth? Are not all these things that you see the offspring of one mother, earth? Why, then, O vain and empty-minded — for I will say it again — having blasphemed the region above the heavens, have you dragged piety down to the ground, fashioning for yourselves chthonic gods, and, pursuing these created things in preference to the uncreated God, fallen into deeper gloom?

The Parian stone is fair, but it is not yet Poseidon; the ivory is fair, but it is not yet the Olympian. Matter is always in need of art, but God is without need. Art has come forward, matter has been clothed with the shape; and the richness of the substance, fit for gain, becomes worthy of worship only through the shape. Your statue is gold, it is wood, it is stone, it is earth, if you consider it from above — earth that has received its form from the craftsman. But I have learned to tread the earth, not to worship it; for it is not lawful for me ever to entrust the hopes of the soul to lifeless things. We must, then, go as close as possible to the statues, that their error may be convicted out of their very appearance as native to them; for the forms of the statues have stamped upon them very plainly the character of the demons. If, then, one were to go round and gaze upon the paintings and the statues, he would at once recognize your gods from their disgraceful figures: Dionysus from his dress, Hephaestus from his craft, Deo from her calamity, Ino from her veil, Poseidon from his trident, Zeus from his swan; the pyre points to Heracles; and if one sees a naked woman painted, he understands the golden Aphrodite. Thus that Cyprian, Pygmalion, fell in love with an ivory statue; the statue was of Aphrodite, and it was naked; the Cyprian is overcome by the figure and unites with the statue — and this Philostephanus records. And another Aphrodite in Cnidus was stone, and was fair; another man fell in love with this one and united with the stone — Posidippus records it, the former in his work on Cyprus, the latter in his work on Cnidus. So strong was art to deceive, becoming a pander to amorous men, leading them into the pit. Productive indeed is the craftsman's art, but it cannot deceive a rational man, nor those who have lived according to reason. Doves, indeed, flew to painted doves because of the likeness, and horses neighed at well-painted mares; they say a maiden fell in love with an image, and a fair youth with the Cnidian statue — but the eyes of the spectators were deceived by the art. For no man in his right mind would have embraced a goddess, or been buried with a corpse, or fallen in love with a demon and a stone. But you art deceives by another sorcery: even if it does not lead you to love, yet it does lead you to honour and worship the statues and the paintings. The painting is like, indeed: let the art be praised, but let it not deceive man as though it were truth. The horse stands quietly, the dove is still, the wing inactive; but the cow of Daedalus, made of wood, drew a wild bull to her, and the art, deceiving him, forced the beast to mount a woman in love. So great a frenzy did the arts, working their evil arts, breed in the senseless. But the keepers and tenders of apes have marvelled that no waxen or clay likeness or doll deceives these creatures; yet you, then, will become worse even than apes, clinging to little statues of stone and wood and gold and ivory, and to paintings. The makers of such ruinous playthings for you are the stone-cutters and the statue-makers, the painters too and the carpenters and the poets, who bring in a great rabble of such things: in the fields Satyrs and Pans, in the woods the Nymphs of the mountains and the Hamadryads, yes, and about the waters and the rivers and the springs the Naiads, and about the sea the Nereids. And by now the magi boast of demons as ministers of their own impiety, having enrolled them as their own servants, having made them by their incantations into slaves under compulsion. The marriages, then, of gods, and the begettings of children, and the childbirths recorded, and the adulteries sung, and the feastings made matter of comedy, and the laughter brought in over the wine — all these urge me to cry out, even though I would be silent: Alas for the godlessness! You have made heaven a stage, and the divine has become for you a drama, and the holy you have made a comedy with the masks of demons, satirizing true piety with superstition. "Then the harper struck up to sing a fair song" — sing to us, Homer, the fair strain — "of the love of Ares and fair-crowned Aphrodite, how first they lay together secretly in the house of Hephaestus; and much he gave, and shamed the bed and couch of the lord Hephaestus." Stop the song, Homer; it is not fair, it teaches adultery; and we have refused even our ears to fornication; for we — we are they who carry about the image of God in this living and moving statue, man — an indwelling image, a counsellor, a companion, a sharer of the hearth, sympathetic, more than sympathetic; we have become an offering to God for Christ's sake. We are "the elect race, the royal priesthood, a holy nation, a peculiar people, who once were no people, but now are the people of God"; we who, according to John, "are not of those below," but have learned the whole from him who came from above; who have understood the dispensation of God; who have practised to walk in newness of life. But the many do not think these things; casting away shame and fear, they inscribe at home the lewd doings of the demons. Indeed, fixing their gaze on certain painted tablets hung up rather high, they have adorned their bedchambers with wantonness, reckoning licentiousness piety; and reclining upon their couches, in the very midst of their embraces, they look up at that naked Aphrodite, bound fast in her embrace, and at the amorous bird flitting about Leda; and, approving the picture of the female, they impress it on their seal-rings, using a seal suited to the licentiousness of Zeus. These are the archetypes of your luxury, these the theologies of outrage, these the teachings of the gods who join with you in fornication; for "what each man wishes, that also he thinks," according to the Athenian orator. And of what sort, again, are your other images — little Pans and naked girls and drunken Satyrs and swollen members, laid bare in the paintings, convicted of their incontinence? And now, openly gazing upon the figures of all wantonness, set out for the whole public, you are not ashamed, but keep them up still more, dedicating them, just as, forsooth, you do the images of your gods, consecrating at home pillars of shamelessness, inscribing on equal terms the postures of Philaenis as the labours of Heracles. Of these we proclaim forgetfulness not only of the use, but also of the very sight and hearing. Your ears have played the harlot, your eyes have committed fornication, and — what is stranger — before the embrace your eyes have committed adultery. O you who have done violence to man and struck out the divine impress of his fashioning, you disbelieve everything, that you may give yourselves up to passion; and you believe in the idols, emulating their incontinence, but disbelieve God, not enduring chastity; you have hated the better and honoured the worse, becoming spectators of virtue but contenders for vice. Blessed alone, then, so to speak, are all those, of one mind, of whom the Sibyl says, "who shall deny all temples when they see them, and altars, vain shrines of dumb stones, and stone xoana and statues made with hands, defiled with living blood and with sacrifices of four-footed creatures, of two-footed, of winged things, and with the slaughter of beasts." For indeed it has been forbidden us to ply openly a deceiving art: "you shall not make," says the prophet, "the likeness of anything that is in heaven above or that is in the earth beneath." Could we, then, still suppose Praxiteles' Demeter and Kore and the mystic Iacchus to be gods, or the arts of Lysippus, or the hands of Apelles, which have clothed matter with the appearance of divine glory? But you, that the statue may be wrought as comely as possible, persevere; yet that you may not yourselves, through insensibility, be made like to the statues, you take no thought. Very plainly and briefly does the prophetic word convict custom, saying that "all the gods of the nations are idols of demons; but God made the heavens" and the things in heaven. Some, then, wandering from this point, somehow worship divine art, but not God — the sun and moon and the rest of the choir of the stars — supposing these, against all reason, to be gods, the very instruments of time. "For by his word were they established, and by the breath of his mouth is all their host." But human art makes houses and ships and cities and pictures; and how could I tell all that God makes? Behold the whole world: it is his work; and heaven and the sun and the angels and men are the works of his fingers. How great is the power of God! His mere will is the making of a world; for God alone made it, since he alone is truly God. By his mere willing he creates, and on his mere willing follows the coming-to-be. Here the chorus of philosophers turns aside, agreeing that man has been made altogether fair for the spectacle of heaven, yet worshipping the things that appear in heaven and are grasped by sight. For even if the works in heaven are not human, yet they have been made for men. And let none of you worship the sun, but let him long for the maker of the sun; let none deify the world, but let him seek after the maker of the world. The only refuge, it seems, left to him who is to come to the doors of salvation is divine wisdom; from this, as from some inviolable sanctuary, man can no longer be carried off by any of the demons, as he hastens to salvation.

Let us now run over, if you will, the opinions of the philosophers too, all that they boast about the gods, that we may find whether philosophy itself, for vainglory's sake, makes matter into an idol, or whether, in passing, we can show it deifying certain spirits, dreaming the truth. The elements, then, some set down as first principles, hymning them: Thales of Miletus, water; and Anaximenes, himself also a Milesian, air, whom Diogenes of Apollonia afterward followed. Parmenides the Eleatic introduced as gods fire and earth; but one of these only, fire, Hippasus of Metapontum and Heraclitus of Ephesus supposed to be a god. As for Empedocles of Acragas, he fell into a plurality, and in addition to these four elements reckons up Strife and Love. These too, then, are godless, who, by a certain unwise wisdom, worship matter; and though they do not honour stones or timber, they deify earth, the mother of these; and though they do not fashion a Poseidon, they bow down to water itself. For what is Poseidon but a certain liquid substance, named from "drinking" (posis)? Just as, of course, the warlike Ares is named from "lifting up" (arsis) and "destruction" (anairesis), by which it seems to me that many, especially those who simply fix a sword and sacrifice to it as to Ares — and this is a Scythian custom, as Eudoxus says in the second book of his Circuit of the Earth; and of the Scythians, the Sauromatae, as Hicesius says in his work On Mysteries, reverence the scimitar. This too is the case with the followers of Heraclitus, who reverence fire as the primal element; for this fire others have named Hephaestus. And the magi of the Persians have honoured fire, and many of the inhabitants of Asia, and besides them the Macedonians, as Diogenes says in the first book of his Persian Affairs. Why need I list the Sauromatae, whom Nymphodorus in his Barbarian Customs records as reverencing fire, or the Persians and the Medes and the magi? Dinon says that these sacrifice in the open air, reckoning fire and water alone as the statues of the gods. Nor did I conceal their ignorance either. For even if they think they are most of all escaping error, yet they slide into another deception: statues of gods they have not supposed to be wood and stones, like the Greeks, nor ibises and ichneumons, like the Egyptians, but fire and water, like philosophers. After many cycles of years, however, they too came to reverence statues of human form, as Berossus shows in the third book of his Chaldaic Affairs, this having been introduced by Artaxerxes son of Darius son of Ochus, who first set up the statue of Aphrodite Anaïtis in Babylon and Susa and Ecbatana, and showed the Persians and Bactrians and Damascus and Sardis to reverence it. Let the philosophers, then, confess that their teachers are the Persians or the Sauromatae or the magi, from whom they have learned the godlessness of the principles they reverence, ignorant of the ruler who is the maker of all things and the fashioner of those principles themselves — the God without beginning — while they turn to those poor and weak elements, as the apostle says, made for the service of men. And of the other philosophers, all who, passing beyond the elements, busied themselves with something loftier and more extraordinary, some of them hymned the Infinite, as Anaximander (he was a Milesian) and Anaxagoras of Clazomenae and the Athenian Archelaus. These two, indeed, both set Mind over the Infinite; but Leucippus the Milesian and Metrodorus of Chios, it seems, left two principles also, the full and the void; and Democritus of Abdera, taking these two, added the images. For Alcmaeon of Croton thought the stars were gods, being ensouled. I will not pass over their shamelessness: Xenocrates (this man was a Chalcedonian) hints at seven gods, the planets, and an eighth, the world composed of all the fixed stars. Nor indeed will I pass by the Stoics, who say that the divine pervades all matter, even the meanest, who simply disgrace philosophy. Nor do I think it hard, now that I have come to this point, to make mention also of those of the Peripatos; and the father of the school, not understanding the Father of all things, thinks that the one called "Supreme" is the soul of the universe; that is, supposing the soul of the world to be God, he is pierced by his own argument. For he who limits providence as far as the moon herself, and then reckons the world a god, overturns himself, dogmatizing a god that has no share in God. And that Eresian, Theophrastus, the pupil of Aristotle, sometimes suspects heaven, sometimes spirit, to be God. Of Epicurus alone I will willingly be forgetful, who thinks that God cares for nothing, being impious through and through. And what of Heraclides of Pontus? Is there any point where he too is not dragged down to the images of Democritus?

And a great rabble of such men flows in upon me, bringing in, like some hobgoblin, a strange shadow-painting of foreign demons, mythologizing with old wives' twaddle. Far be it from us to permit men to listen to such tales, men whom we do not accustom even to soothe our own children with myths when they cry, as the saying goes, dreading to nurse up in them the godlessness proclaimed by these would-be wise men, who know the truth no better than babes. For why, in the name of truth, do you show those who have believed you to be subject to flux and motion and disorderly eddies? Why do you fill my life with idols, fashioning into gods winds or air or fire or earth or stones or timber or iron — this world of ours — and making gods too of the planets, prating astrology, not astronomy, to men truly led astray, with this much-bruited star-talk? I long for the Lord of the winds, the Lord of fire, the maker of the world, the kindler of the sun's light; I seek after God, not the works of God. Whom, then, shall I take from you as a fellow-worker in the search? For we have not utterly despaired of you. If you will, take Plato. Where, then, must we track God, O Plato? "For it is a task to find the father and maker of this universe, and, having found him, it is impossible to declare him to all." Why so, in the name of God himself? "Because it can in no wise be spoken." Well said, Plato; you have touched upon the truth. But do not weary; lay hold with me of the search concerning the Good; for into all men without exception, but especially those who spend their lives in discourse, there has been instilled a certain divine effluence. Wherefore, even unwillingly, they confess that there is one God, imperishable and unbegotten, somewhere up above, about the back of heaven, in his own proper watch-tower, truly existing forever. "But what kind of God should one conceive? Him who sees all things, while himself unseen," says Euripides. Menander, then, seems to me to have gone astray, where he says: "O Sun, you must worship first of the gods, through whom it is possible to behold the other gods." For not even the sun could ever show the true God; but the sound Reason, which is the sun of the soul, alone — through which alone, when it has risen within, in the depth of the mind — its eye is illumined. Hence not unreasonably did Democritus say that "few of the men of reason, stretching out their hands to this place which we Greeks now call air, said that all this was Zeus; and he knows all things and gives all and takes away, and he is king of all." In this way, too, Plato, thinking of God, hints at him: "About the king of all are all things, and that is the cause of all fair things." Who, then, is the king of all? God, the measure of the truth of the things that are. As, then, the things measured are grasped by the measure, so too, by the understanding of God, the truth is measured and grasped. And the truly holy Moses says: "There shall not be in your bag a weight and a weight, great or small; nor shall there be in your house a measure great or small; but you shall have a true and just weight" — taking God to be the weight and measure and number of all things. For the unjust and unequal idols are hidden away at home, in the bag and in the soul that is, so to speak, filthy; but the only just measure, the only truly existing God, ever equal in the same way and after the same manner, measures all things and weighs them, encompassing and upholding without bias, as in the balance of justice, the nature of the universe. "God, then, as the ancient saying goes, holding the beginning and end and middle of all things that are, completes a straight course, journeying round according to nature; and ever upon him follows Justice, the avenger of those who fall short of the divine law." Whence, O Plato, do you hint at the truth? Whence does the unstinted supply of your words prophesy piety? "Wiser than these," he says, "are the races of the barbarians." I know your teachers, even if you wish to conceal them: geometry you learn from the Egyptians, astronomy from the Babylonians, the wholesome incantations you take from the Thracians; the Assyrians too have taught you much; but the laws, all that are true, and the right opinion concerning God, you have profited from the Hebrews themselves, "who not with empty deceits, nor with works of men — gold and bronze and silver and ivory, and idols of wood and of stone, of dead mortals — do they pay honour, all that mortals do in their empty-minded counsel; but they raise to heaven pure arms, rising at dawn from their beds, ever purifying their flesh with water, and they honour the One alone who ever rules, the immortal." And do not, O Philosophy, set before me this one Plato only, but be eager to bring forward many others too, who declare the one and only true God to be God, by his inspiration, if anywhere they have laid hold on the truth. For Antisthenes thought this — not as a Cynic, but as a pupil of Socrates — that God is like to no one; wherefore no one can learn him from an image. And Xenophon the Athenian would himself also have written something expressly, bearing witness about the truth as Socrates did, had he not feared the poison of Socrates; yet none the less he hints: "He who shakes all things and brings them to rest is manifest as some great and powerful one; but of what form he is, is unseen; nor indeed does the sun, that seems all-shining, seem to permit itself to be looked at, but if anyone shamelessly gazes at it, it takes away his sight." Whence, then, does the son of Gryllus draw his wisdom? Plainly from the prophetess of the Hebrews, who prophesies somewhat thus: "What flesh can with its eyes behold the heavenly and true immortal God, who dwells in the pole? Nay, men, born mortal, cannot even stand against the rays of the sun." Cleanthes of Pedasus, the philosopher of the Stoa, shows not a poetic theogony, but a true theology. He did not conceal what he had in mind concerning God: "Do you ask me what the Good is like? Listen, then: ordered, just, holy, pious, master of itself, useful, fair, fitting, austere, self-contained, ever profitable, fearless, griefless, advantageous, painless, helpful, pleasing, secure, friendly, honoured, agreeing, glorious, free from conceit, careful, gentle, vehement, lasting, blameless, ever abiding. Every man is base who looks to glory, as though he would get from her some fair thing." Here, I think, he clearly teaches what God is, and how common opinion and custom enslave those who follow them, but not those who seek after God. Nor must we conceal the followers of Pythagoras, who say: "God is one; and this God is not, as some suppose, outside the world-order, but within it, whole in the whole circle, overseer of all coming-to-be, the blending of all the ages and the worker of his own powers and of all works, the light-giver in heaven and father of all, mind and the ensouling of the whole circle, the mover of all things." Enough is even this for the knowledge of God, written down by them through the inspiration of God, and selected by us, for one able to discern the truth even a little.

Now let there come to us — for philosophy alone is not sufficient — poetry too, which has busied itself wholly about falsehood, at last, late as it is, to bear witness to the truth, or rather to confess to God its mythical wandering. Let whatever poet wishes come forward first. Aratus, then, understands the power of God to pervade all things: "that all things may grow firm; therefore him men ever propitiate first and last. Hail, Father, great wonder, great boon to men." In this way too the Ascraean Hesiod hints at God: "For he himself is king and lord of all, and of the immortals none else has matched his might." Even upon the stage they lay bare the truth: the one — "looking up to the ether and to heaven, hold this to be God," says Euripides. And Sophocles son of Sophillus: "In truth there is one God, one, who made heaven and the wide earth and the gleaming swell of the sea and the force of the winds; but mortals, much wandering in heart, set up for ourselves, as a comfort in griefs, statues of the gods from stones, or figures wrought of bronze or gold or ivory; and rendering to these sacrifices and empty festivals, we suppose that thus we are pious." This poet, then, has now, and even at some risk, brought the truth onto the stage before the spectators.

And the Thracian hierophant and poet at once, Orpheus son of Oeagrus, after his initiation into the orgies and his theology of the idols, brings in a recantation of truth, singing the truly sacred discourse, late at last, yet for all that singing it: "I will speak to those for whom it is lawful; but set up the doors, all you profane alike. But you, hearken, son of light-bringing Mene, Musaeus; for I will declare what is true. And let not the things that before appeared in your breast rob you of your dear life. Looking to the divine Word, attend to it, guiding straight the understanding vessel of the heart; and tread well the path, and look on him alone, the immortal King of the world." Then, going on, he expressly adds: "He is one, self-begotten; from one are all things begotten; and in them he himself moves about; and no mortal beholds him, but he himself beholds all." So, then, Orpheus; in time, at last, having wandered, he came to understand. But do not you, mortal of crafty mind, delay and tarry; but, turning back from your wandering, propitiate God. For even if the Greeks, having got certain sparks of the divine Word, uttered some few things of the truth, they bear witness indeed to its power, that it is not hidden, but they convict themselves as weak, not having reached the end. For by now, I think, it has become plain to everyone that those who do or say anything apart from the Word of truth are like men forced to walk without a footing.

And the very refutations of your gods, which the poets, constrained by truth, put into comedy, may shame you into salvation. Menander the comic poet, for instance, in the play The Charioteer: "No god pleases me," he says, "who goes about outside with an old woman, nor who slips into houses upon a little board" — for such are the begging priests of the Mother. Hence Antisthenes reasonably said to them as they begged: "I do not feed the Mother of the gods, whom the gods feed." Again the same comic poet, in the play The Priestess, vexed at the custom, tries to convict the godless conceit of error, adding sensibly: "For if a man by his cymbals drags the god where he wishes, then he who does this is greater than the god; but these are instruments of recklessness and of livelihood, devised by men." And not Menander only, but Homer too and Euripides and many other poets convict your gods, and do not fear to revile them, even to no small degree. At once they call Athena "dog-fly" and Hephaestus "lame in both legs"; and to Aphrodite Helen says, "Mayest thou never return on thy feet to Olympus." And of Dionysus Homer writes openly: "who once chased the nurses of frenzied Dionysus down through holy Nysa; and they all together cast their wands to the ground, beneath the murderous Lycurgus." Worthy in truth of a Socratic schooling is Euripides, looking to the truth and despising the spectators; now convicting Apollo, "who dwells at the central seat, dealing out to mortals utterance most clear" — "obeying him, I slew my mother; hold him impious and slay him; he erred, not I, being more ignorant than the fair and the just" — now bringing in Heracles mad, and elsewhere drunken and insatiable. For how should he not be? — who, feasting on the flesh, "ate green figs upon it, howling without music, so as to be understood even by a barbarian." And in the play Ion he wheels out the gods bare-headed to the theatre: "How, then, is it just that you who wrote the laws for mortals should yourselves incur a charge of injustice? But if — for it shall not be, yet I will use the argument — you shall pay penalty to men for forced unions, you and Poseidon and Zeus who rules heaven, you shall empty your temples in paying for your injustices."

It is time now, then — the rest being already gone through in order — to come to the prophetic Scriptures. For the oracles too, holding out to us most plainly the starting-points toward piety, lay the foundation of the truth. And the divine Scriptures and sober ways of life are short roads of salvation; bare of cosmetic art and of outward fine speech and chatter and flattery, they raise up the man choked by wickedness, despising the slipperiness of worldly life, with one and the same voice healing many things, turning us away from harmful deception, and openly exhorting us to manifest salvation. At once, then, let the prophetess Sibyl first sing for us the song of salvation: "Behold, this one is clear to all, free from error: come, pursue not darkness and gloom forever. Behold, the sweet-eyed light of the sun shines surpassingly. Know, laying up wisdom in your breasts: there is one God, who sends rains and winds and earthquakes, lightnings, famines, plagues and grievous sorrows, and snows and the rest. Why should I recount them one by one? He rules heaven, he holds sway over earth, himself from the beginning." Very inspiredly, likening deception to darkness and the knowledge of God to the sun and light, and setting both side by side in comparison, she teaches the choice. For falsehood is not dispelled by the bare setting beside it of the truth, but, being driven out by the use of the truth, it is put to flight. Jeremiah the all-wise prophet, or rather the Holy Spirit in Jeremiah, shows God: "I am a God at hand," he says, "and not a God afar off. If a man does anything in secret, shall I not see him? Do I not fill the heavens and the earth? says the Lord." And again, through Isaiah: "Who has measured," he says, "the heaven with a span and all the earth with the hollow of his hand?" Behold the greatness of God, and be amazed. Him let us worship, of whom the prophet says: "At your presence the mountains shall melt, as wax melts at the presence of fire." This, he says, is the God whose throne is heaven and footstool the earth; who, if he should open the heaven, trembling shall seize you. Do you wish to hear too what this prophet says about the idols? "They shall be made a public example before the sun, and their carcasses shall be food for the birds of heaven and the beasts of the earth, and they shall rot under the sun and the moon, which they themselves loved and to which they were enslaved, and their city shall be burned." And he says that the elements too and the world shall be destroyed together with them: "The earth," he says, "shall grow old, and the heaven shall pass away, but the word of the Lord abides forever." And what when again God wishes to show himself through Moses? "See, see that I am, and there is no other God beside me. I will slay and I will make alive; I will smite and I will heal, and there is none who can deliver out of my hands." But do you wish to hear too another oracle-singer? You have the whole prophetic choir, the fellow-revellers of Moses. What does the Holy Spirit say to them through Hosea? I will not shrink to tell it: "Behold, I am he that establishes thunder and creates wind, whose hands have founded the host of heaven." And again, through Isaiah — and this saying too I will recall to you — "I am, I am," he says, "the Lord, who speaks righteousness and announces truth. Gather yourselves and come; take counsel together, you that are saved from the nations. They have no knowledge, those who lift up the carved wood of theirs, and pray to gods who cannot save them." Then, going on: "I," he says, "am God, and there is none righteous beside me, and there is no saviour beside me. Turn to me and be saved, you from the ends of the earth. I am God, and there is none other; by myself I swear." And against the idolaters he is indignant, saying: "To whom have you likened the Lord? Or to what likeness have you likened him? Has a carpenter made an image, or has a goldsmith, having melted gold, gilded it over?" — and what follows. Are you, then, still idolaters? But even now beware the threats; for the carved images and the works of hands shall howl — or rather those who trust in them, for the matter is insensible. Again he says: "The Lord shall shake the inhabited cities, and shall lay hold of the whole world in his hand like a nest." Why should I declare to you the mysteries of wisdom, and sayings from a Hebrew child made wise? "The Lord created me as the beginning of his ways for his works"; and the Lord gives wisdom, and from his presence come knowledge and understanding. "How long, O sluggard, will you lie down? When will you be raised from sleep? But if you are unsluggish, your harvest shall come to you like a fountain" — the fatherly Word, the good lamp, the Lord who brings the light, faith and salvation to all. "For the Lord who made the earth in his strength," as Jeremiah says, "set up the world in his wisdom." For us, when we had fallen away to the idols, wisdom, which is his Word, sets us upright again toward the truth. And this is the first resurrection from our falling. Whence, turning men away from all idolatry, the inspired Moses cried out most nobly: "Hear, O Israel; the Lord your God, the Lord is one, and you shall worship the Lord your God and serve him alone." Now then, understand, O men, according to that blessed psalmist David: "Lay hold of instruction, lest at any time the Lord be angry, and you perish from the righteous way, when his wrath is quickly kindled. Blessed are all they that trust in him." And already, taking exceeding pity on us, the Lord gives the saving strain, like a marching rhythm: "Sons of men, how long will you be heavy of heart? Why do you love vanity and seek after a lie?" What, then, is the vanity and what the lie? The holy apostle of the Lord, charging the Greeks, will explain to you: "Because, knowing God, they glorified him not as God, neither were thankful, but became vain in their reasonings, and changed the glory of God into the likeness of an image of corruptible man, and served the creature rather than the Creator." And surely this God it is "who in the beginning made the heaven and the earth"; but you do not understand God, and you worship heaven; and how are you not impious? Hear again the prophet saying: "The sun shall fail and the heaven shall be darkened; but the Almighty shall shine forever, and the powers of the heavens shall be shaken, and the heavens shall be rolled together like a scroll, stretched out and contracted" — for these are the prophetic voices — "and the earth shall flee from the face of the Lord."

And I could bring to you ten thousand Scriptures, of which "not one tittle shall pass away" without being fulfilled; for the mouth of the Lord, the Holy Spirit, has spoken these things. "No longer, then," he says, "my son, despise the instruction of the Lord, nor faint when you are rebuked by him." O the exceeding love toward man! Not as a teacher to disciples, nor as a master to servants, nor as God to men, but "as a gentle father he admonishes his sons." Then Moses confesses that he is afraid and trembling, hearing about the Word; but you, hearing the divine Word, do you not fear? Are you not in anguish? Are you not at once cautious and eager to learn thoroughly — that is, eager for salvation — fearing wrath, loving grace, emulating hope, that you may escape the judgement? Come, come, O my young company; for unless you become again as little children and are born anew, as the Scripture says, you shall not receive the Father who truly is, nor shall you ever enter into the kingdom of the heavens. For how is the stranger permitted to enter? But when, I think, he is enrolled and made a citizen and receives the Father, then he shall be among the things of the Father, then he shall be deemed worthy to inherit, then he shall share in the Father's kingdom with the genuine, the beloved Son. For this is the Church of the firstborn, composed of many good children; these are the firstborn enrolled in heaven, who keep festival with so many myriads of angels. And we are the firstborn children, the nurslings of God, the genuine friends of the Firstborn, the first of all other men to have understood God, the first to have been torn away from sins, the first to have been separated from the devil. But now some are godless in proportion as God is loving to man; for he wishes us, who were slaves, to become sons, but they have disdained even to become sons. O the great folly! You are ashamed of the Lord. He promises freedom, but you run away into slavery. He gives salvation as a gift, but you are carried down to death. He bestows eternal life, but you await punishment, and prefer the fire which the Lord has prepared for the devil and his angels. For this cause the blessed apostle says: "I testify in the Lord that you no longer walk as the nations walk, in the vanity of their mind, being darkened in their understanding and alienated from the life of God, through the ignorance that is in them, through the hardness of their heart; who, being past feeling, have given themselves over to wantonness, to work all uncleanness and greed." When such a witness convicts the folly of men and calls upon God, what else remains for the unbelieving but judgement and condemnation? And the Lord does not weary of exhorting, of striking fear, of urging, of rousing, of admonishing; indeed he wakes men from sleep, and raises up out of their darkness those who have gone astray: "Awake," he says, "you that sleep, and arise from the dead, and Christ the Lord shall give you light" — the sun of the resurrection, "begotten before the morning star," who has bestowed life by his own rays. Let no one, then, despise the Word, lest he unawares despise himself. For the Scripture somewhere says: "Today, if you will hear his voice, harden not your hearts, as in the provocation, in the day of temptation in the wilderness, where your fathers tempted me in a testing." And if you wish to learn what the testing is, the Holy Spirit will explain it to you: "And I saw my works," he says, "forty years; wherefore I was grieved with that generation and said, They do always err in heart; but they have not known my ways; so I swore in my wrath, If they shall enter into my rest." See the threat; see the exhortation; see the honour. Why, then, do we still change grace into wrath, and not, with open ears, receive the Word, and lodge God in pure souls? For great is the grace of his promise, "if today we hear his voice"; and that "today" is increased day by day, as long as it is called "today." And until the consummation both the "today" and the learning abide; and then the true "today," the unfailing day of God, is stretched out coextensive with the ages. Let us, then, ever hearken to the voice of the divine Word; for the "today" is an image of the eternal age, and the day is a symbol of light, and the Word is light to men, through whom we are illumined toward God. Reasonably, then, to those who believe and obey, grace shall abound exceedingly; but to those who disobey and wander in heart, and have not known the ways of the Lord, which John commanded to make straight and prepare, with these God is grieved and threatens. And indeed the end of the threat, as the elders among the Hebrews who wandered say enigmatically, the threat — for they are said not to enter into the rest because of unbelief, until, following the successor of Moses, they learned at last by experience that they could not otherwise be saved than by believing as Jesus did. And the Lord, being loving to man, calls all men to the knowledge of the truth, he who sends the Comforter. What, then, is the knowledge? Piety; and "piety is profitable unto all things," according to Paul, "having promise of the life that now is and of that which is to come." At what price would you have confessed, O men, that you would buy eternal salvation, if it were for sale? Not even if one were to measure out the whole Pactolus, the fabled stream of gold, would he count out a worthy price for salvation. Do not, then, grow weary; it is possible for you, if you will, to buy out the precious salvation with your own treasure, with love and faith, which is a price worthy of life. This price God gladly receives. "For we have hoped in the living God, who is the saviour of all men, especially of the faithful." But the rest, grown fast to the world like seaweed on sea-girt rocks, make light of immortality, like the old man of Ithaca, longing not for the truth and the heavenly fatherland, and besides for the light that truly is, but for the smoke.

Piety, then, making man like to God so far as is possible, inscribes God as a fitting teacher, who alone is able worthily to make man like to God. This teaching the apostle, knowing it to be truly divine, "you, O Timothy," he says, "from a babe have known the sacred writings, which are able to make you wise unto salvation through faith in Christ." For truly sacred are the writings that make holy and make divine; out of which writings and sacred syllables the same apostle accordingly calls the composed Scriptures, the books, "inspired of God," being profitable for teaching, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness, that the man of God may be perfect, furnished completely unto every good work. No one would be so astonished at the exhortations of the other saints as at the Lord himself, the lover of man; for he has no other work but this alone, to save man. He cries, at any rate, pressing on to salvation: "The kingdom of the heavens is at hand"; he turns men about as they draw near by fear. In this way too the apostle of the Lord, exhorting the Macedonians, becomes an interpreter of the divine voice: "The Lord is at hand," he says; "take heed lest we be found empty." But you are so fearless — or rather faithless — obeying neither the Lord himself nor Paul, and that though he was bound for Christ's sake. "Taste and see that the Lord is good." Faith will lead you in, experience will teach you, the Scripture will train you, saying: "Come, O children, hearken to me; I will teach you the fear of the Lord." Then, as to those who already believe, it briefly adds: "Who is the man that desires life, that loves to see good days?" It is we, we shall say, the worshippers of the Good, the emulators of good things. Hear, then, you that are far off; hear, you that are near: the Word is hidden from none; it is a common light, it shines upon all men; there is no Cimmerian in the Word. Let us hasten to salvation, to the new birth; let us hasten to be gathered, the many, into one love, according to the union of the single substance. Working good in like manner, let us pursue unity, seeking out the good Monad. And the union out of many, having received divine harmony out of the many-voiced and scattered, becomes one symphony, following one leader of the chorus and teacher, the Word, resting upon the very truth, saying "Abba, Father." This true voice God welcomes, receiving it first from his own children as firstfruits.

"But," you say, "it is not reasonable to overthrow a custom handed down to us from our fathers." Then why do we not use our first food, milk, to which the nurses no doubt accustomed us from birth? Why do we increase or diminish the paternal estate, and not keep it equal, as we received it? Why do we no longer dribble into our fathers' bosoms, or do the other things which, when we were infants and were reared by our mothers, made us a laughing-stock? Why did we correct ourselves, even if we did not happen upon good tutors? Then, on voyages, deviations, though harmful and dangerous, yet somehow fall out pleasantly; but in life shall we not forsake the custom that is wicked and passion-ridden and godless, even though our fathers be angry, and turn aside toward the truth and seek after the Father who truly is, thrusting away custom like a deadly drug? For this very thing is the fairest of the tasks before us, to show you that it was from madness and from this thrice-wretched custom that piety came to be hated. For so great a good — than which nothing greater has yet been given by God to the begetting of men — would never have been hated or forbidden, unless you, swept along by custom, then, stopping your ears against us, like stiff-necked horses balking, biting on the bit, fled from our words, longing to shake us off, your charioteers of life, and, carried by your folly toward the cliffs of destruction, supposed the holy Word of God to be accursed. There follows for you, then, according to Sophocles, the wage of your choice: "mind gone, ears useless, empty thoughts." And you do not know that this, above all, is true: that the good and pious shall obtain a good requital, having honoured the Good, while the wicked, on the contrary, shall obtain the fitting punishment; and upon the ruler of wickedness chastisement is hung. The prophet Zechariah threatens him: "The Lord who chose Jerusalem rebuke you. Is not this a brand plucked out of the fire?" What craving, then, still lies in men for a voluntary death? Why have they fled to this death-bringing brand, with which they shall be burned up, when it is possible to live well according to God, not according to custom? For God bestows life, but a wicked custom, after the departure from this world, brings empty repentance together with punishment. "And the foolish learns by suffering" that superstition destroys and piety saves. Let one of you look at those who serve the idols, with filthy hair, outraged in dingy and torn raiment, wholly untried in baths, savage with the points of their nails; many, too, deprived of their privy parts, showing in fact that the precincts of the idols are tombs or prison-houses. These seem to me to be mourning, not worshipping, the gods, having suffered things worthy of pity rather than of piety. And, seeing these things, are you still blind, and will you not look up to the Lord of all and Master of the universe? Will you not flee, escaping from these prison-houses here, to the mercy from heaven? For God, out of his great love toward man, holds fast to man, as the mother-bird flies down after the nestling that falls out of the nest; and if some creeping beast should gape at the nestling, "the mother flutters round, bewailing her dear young." God the Father both seeks his creature and heals the fall and drives away the beast and takes up the nestling again, urging it to fly back to the nest. Then, dogs that have lost their way, hunting by scent, have tracked out their master; and horses, having thrown their rider, have obeyed their master at a single whistle. "The ox knows," it says, "his owner, and the ass his master's crib; but Israel has not known me." What, then, the Lord? He does not bear malice; he still pities, he still demands repentance. And I wish to ask you, whether it does not seem to you absurd that you men, having been made the creature of God and having received your soul from him and being wholly his, should serve another master, and besides should worship instead of the king the tyrant, and instead of the good the wicked. For who, in the name of truth, being of sound mind, forsakes the good and consorts with wickedness? Who is there that, fleeing from God, lives with demons? Who, being able to be a son of God, takes pleasure in being a slave? Or who, being able to be a citizen of heaven, pursues the gloom, when he might till paradise and walk about heaven and partake of the living and pure fountain, treading the air in the track of that shining cloud, like Elijah, beholding the saving rain? But these, wallowing like worms about pools and mire, the streams of pleasure, feed upon profitless and senseless luxuries, swinish men. "For swine," it says, "delight in mire rather than in pure water," and "rave over filth," according to Democritus. Let us not, then, let us not be enslaved nor become swinish, but, as true children of the light, let us look up and gaze toward the light, lest the Lord prove us bastards, as the sun does the eagles. Let us repent, then, and pass over from unlearning to knowledge, from folly to understanding, from incontinence to self-control, from injustice to righteousness, from godlessness to God. Fair is the risk of deserting to God. And there are many other goods, too, for the lovers of righteousness to enjoy, who pursue eternal salvation — yes, and those which God himself hints at, speaking through Isaiah: "There is an inheritance for those who serve the Lord." Fair indeed and lovely is the inheritance — not gold, not silver, not raiment, the things of the earth, where the moth and the robber lurk, with eyes set upon the low-lying wealth — but that treasure of salvation, to which we must hasten, becoming lovers of the Word. From here our good works set out with us, and fly together with us on the wing of truth. This inheritance the eternal covenant of God puts into our hands, supplying the eternal gift; and this our loving Father, the true Father, does not cease to exhort, to admonish, to instruct, to love; for neither does he cease to save, but counsels the best: "Become just," says the Lord; "you that thirst, go to the water; and as many of you as have no money, come and buy and drink without money." To the bath, to salvation, to the illumination he calls, all but crying out and saying: "Earth I give you and sea, O child, and heaven, and all the living creatures in them I bestow upon you. Only, O child, thirst for the Father; God shall be shown to you without price; the truth is not bought and sold. He gives you the winged things and the swimming things and the things upon the earth; these the Father has fashioned for your thankful enjoyment." With money the bastard, who is the child of destruction, shall buy — he who has chosen to serve mammon; but to you he entrusts what is yours, to you the genuine, I say, who love the Father, for whose sake he still works, and to whom alone he promises, saying: "And the land shall not be sold for confirmation"; for it is not confirmed to corruption; "for all the land is mine," and it is yours too, if you receive God. Whence the Scripture reasonably proclaims good tidings to those who have believed: "But the saints of the Lord shall inherit the glory of God and his power." What glory, O blessed one, tell me? "That which eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has it entered into the heart of man; and they shall rejoice over the kingdom of their Lord forever, Amen." You have, O men, the divine promise of grace; you have heard, too, the other, the threat of punishment, through which the Lord saves, training man by fear and by grace. Why do we delay? Why do we not turn aside from punishment? Why do we not receive the gift? Why do we not choose the better — God instead of the wicked one — and prefer wisdom to idolatry, and take life in exchange for death? "Behold, I have set before your face," he says, "death and life." The Lord tests you, to choose life; he counsels you as a father to obey God. "For if you hear me," he says, "and are willing, you shall eat the good things of the land" — the grace of obedience; "but if you do not hear me nor are willing, the sword and fire shall devour you" — the judgement of disobedience. For "the mouth of the Lord has spoken these things"; the law of truth is the Word of the Lord. Do you wish me to become a good counsellor to you? Then do you hear, and I will show, if I can. You ought, O men, considering the Good itself, to bring to bear an innate faith, a credible witness from within, from your own home, manifestly choosing the best, and not to labour as if it were something to be tracked down. For if one ought to get drunk, say, then one ought to deliberate; but you get drunk before considering; and if one ought to commit outrage, you make no inquiry, but commit outrage with all speed. Only about whether one ought to be pious do you inquire, and whether one ought to follow this wise God and Christ — this you deem worthy of counsel and consideration, not having even understood what befits God, whatever it may be. Believe us, at least, as you believe drunkenness, that you may be sober; believe, at least, as you do outrage, that you may live. But if you wish also to be persuaded, having beheld the manifest faith of the virtues, come, I will set before you, out of my abundance, the persuasion concerning the Word. But you — since now the ancestral customs no longer keep you from the truth, you who have been pre-instructed — you may now hear how the matter stands hereafter. And let no shame at this name forestall you, which "greatly harms men," turning them aside from salvation. Stripping ourselves, then, openly, let us contend genuinely in the stadium of truth, the holy Word being umpire and the Master of all presiding as president of the games. For no small prize lies before us — immortality. Therefore care no more, not even a little, what certain market-rabble say of you, godless dancers in superstition, pushed by folly and madness into the very pit, makers of idols and worshippers of stones. For these have dared to deify men, recording Alexander the Macedonian as a thirteenth god, whom Babylon convicted as a corpse. I admire, then, the Chian sophist, Theocritus by name; after the death of Alexander, mocking the empty opinions of men which they held about gods, Theocritus said to his fellow-citizens: "Men, take courage, so long as you see the gods dying before men."

But he who worships the visible gods and the promiscuous rabble of these created things, and makes them his companions, is far more wretched than those very demons. For God is in no way unjust, as the demons are, but, as far as may be, most just; and there is nothing more like to him than whoever of us becomes most just. "Go forth, then, to the road, all you handicraft folk, who propitiate the grim-eyed Worker-goddess, the daughter of Zeus, with standing winnowing-fans" — you witless makers and worshippers of stones. Let your Pheidias come, and your Polycleitus, and Praxiteles again, and Apelles, and all who pursue the menial crafts, earthy workers of earth. For then, says a certain prophecy, the affairs here shall fare ill, when men trust in statues. Let the petty craftsmen come again, then — for I will not cease from fair speaking. None of these has fashioned a breathing image, nor moulded soft flesh out of earth. Who melted the marrow, or who fixed the bones? Who stretched the sinews? Who blew up the veins? Who poured the blood into them, or who stretched the skin around? Where could any of them make eyes that see? Who breathed in a soul? Who gave righteousness as a gift? Who promised immortality? The Maker of all things alone, the best-craftsman Father, fashioned such a living statue as man. But your Olympian — image of an image, far out of tune with the truth — is a dumb work of Attic hands. For the image of God is his Word — and the genuine Son of the Mind is the divine Word, the archetypal light of light — and the image of the Word is the true man, the mind in man, who is therefore said to have been made "after the image and likeness of God," likened in his heart's understanding to the divine Word, and in this respect rational. But of the visible, earth-born man the earthy image is the man-shaped statue, and it appears far from the truth, a transient impress. Nothing, then, but a life full of madness has seemed to me to have been, when men gave themselves with so much zeal to matter. And custom, fostered by empty opinion, has given you a taste of slavery and of unreasonable curiosity; and the cause is ignorance of lawless and deceitful pretences, which, introducing into the human race the contrivances of ruinous deaths and of hateful idols, having devised many forms of demons, has stamped upon those who follow it a stain of long death. Take, then, the rational water; wash, you that are defiled; sprinkle yourselves clean from custom with the true drops; you must go up pure into the heavens. You are a man — that which is most common; seek out him who made you. You are a son — that which is most peculiarly your own; recognize the Father. But do you still abide in your sins, fast bound by pleasures? To whom will the Lord say, "Yours is the kingdom of the heavens"? Yours it is, if you will, you who have set your choice toward God; yours, if you will only to believe and to follow the brief proclamation, obeying which the Ninevites, by genuine repentance, exchanged the expected capture for the fair salvation. "How, then, shall I go up to the heavens?" you say. The Lord is the way, narrow indeed, but from heaven; narrow indeed, but sending up to the heavens; narrow, despised upon earth; broad, worshipped in the heavens. Then he who has not heard the Word has ignorance as the excuse of his wandering; but he who is struck on the ears, and yet bears to his soul, from his own judgement, disobedience — the wiser he seems to be, the more his understanding turns to his hurt, since he has used his prudence as accuser, not choosing the best; for man is by nature so framed as to be intimate with God. As, then, we do not force the horse to plough nor the bull to hunt, but lead each animal round to that for which it is by nature framed, so, of course, we call man too, born for the contemplation of heaven, a heavenly plant in truth, to the knowledge of God, having grasped what is proper to him and choice and peculiar to him beyond the other animals, a self-sufficient provision for the ages — piety — counselling him to prepare it. Till the soil, we say, if you are a husbandman, but know God while you till; sail, you who love seafaring, but call upon the heavenly Pilot. Has knowledge laid hold of you while you served as a soldier? Hear the general who signals just things.

As, then, men weighed down by sleep and drunkenness, come to your senses, and, looking up a little, consider what the worshipped stones mean for you, and the things you waste with empty zeal upon matter; into ignorance you consume both your goods and your life, as you spend your living upon death, having found this only as the end of your vain hope, not able even to pity yourselves, but not even fit to obey those who pity you for your wandering, enslaved by evil custom, dependent on which of your own accord you are carried to destruction to your last breath; "because the light has come into the world, and men loved darkness rather than the light," when it was possible to wipe away the things that stand in the way of salvation — both conceit and wealth and fear — saying that poetic line: "Whither am I carrying all this wealth? And whither do I myself wander?" Will you not, then, casting away these empty fancies, renounce custom itself, saying to vainglory, "False dreams, farewell; you were nothing after all"?

For what do you think, O men, the Tychon-Hermes is, and that of Andocides, and the Maimed one? Surely it is plain to everyone that they are stones, just as Hermes himself is. And as the halo is not a god, and as the rainbow is not a god, but affections of air and clouds, and as in like manner the day is not a god, nor the year, nor the time made up of these, so neither is the sun nor the moon, by which each of the things named is bounded. Who, then, being of sound mind, would suppose Correction and Punishment and Justice and Nemesis to be gods? For neither are the Erinyes nor the Fates nor Destiny gods, since neither is the state nor glory nor wealth — which painters even show to be blind. But if you deify Modesty and Love and Aphrodite, then let Shame and Impulse and Beauty and Intercourse follow upon them. So Sleep and Death, two twin gods, could no longer reasonably be reckoned by you, these being affections that befall living things naturally; nor will you justly call Doom nor Destiny nor the Fates goddesses. And if Strife and Battle are not gods, neither is Ares nor Enyo. And further, if the lightnings and the thunderbolts and the rains are not gods, how can fire and water be gods? And how the shooting stars and the comets, which come to be through an affection of the air? And he who calls Fortune a god, let him call Action too a god. If, then, none of these is reckoned a god, nor those handmade and insensible fashionings, while a certain providence of a divine power over us is plainly seen, nothing else remains but to confess this — that he alone truly is and subsists, the only truly existing God. But, like men who have drunk mandrake or some other drug, you senseless ones are; and may God grant you one day to come to your senses out of this sleep, and to understand God, and not to imagine gold or stone or tree or action or affection or disease or fear as God. "For thrice ten thousand," in truth, "are upon the bountiful earth" demons — not immortal, nor yet mortal (for they have not even shared in sensation, that they might share in death), but stony and wooden masters of men, outraging and breaking faith with life through custom. "The earth is the Lord's," it says, "and the fullness thereof." Then how dare you, while you revel in what is the Lord's, be ignorant of the Master? "Leave my earth," the Lord will say to you; "touch not the water which I give forth; partake not of the fruits which I till. Render, O man, the price of your nurture to God; recognize your Master; you are God's own creature. But how could his own justly become alien?" For that which is estranged, deprived of intimacy, is deprived of the truth. Are you not, in a manner like Niobe — or rather, to speak more mystically to you, like that Hebrew woman (the men of old called her Lot's wife) — turning to insensibility? We have received that this woman was turned to stone for her love of Sodom; and the Sodomites are the godless and those who turn to impiety, hard-hearted and senseless. Believe that these voices are recited to you from God: do not suppose that stones and timber and birds and serpents are holy, but men not; on the contrary, suppose that men are in truth holy, and that the beasts and stones are what they are. For the wretched and miserable among men believe that God cries out through a raven and a jackdaw, but keeps silence through a man, and they have honoured the raven as a messenger of God, but they hunt down the man of God, who does not croak nor caw, but speaks articulately; alas, who instructs rationally and lovingly — him they undertake to slaughter inhumanly, calling them to righteousness, neither awaiting the grace from above nor turning aside from punishment. For they do not believe God, nor learn his power. But where his love toward man is unspeakable, there his hatred of wickedness is not to be contained. Wrath nourishes the punishment upon sin, but love does good upon repentance. And most pitiable it is to be deprived of the help that comes from God. The blinding of the eyes and the deafening of the hearing is more grievous than the rest of the wicked one's encroachments; for the one is robbed of the heavenly sight, the other deprived of the divine learning. But you, maimed toward the truth, blind in mind and deaf in understanding, are not grieved, are not indignant; you have not desired to see heaven and the maker of heaven, nor sought to hear and learn of the Maker and Father of all things, joining your choice to salvation. For nothing stands in the way of him who hastens toward the knowledge of God — not unlearning, not poverty, not obscurity, not want of possessions. Nor does anyone, having marred the truly true wisdom with bronze, pray to exchange it, nor with iron; for this above all has been well said: "the good man is everywhere saving." For the emulator of the just, as the lover of him who is without need, has little need, having treasured up his blessedness in no other than God himself, where is no moth, no robber, no pirate, but the eternal giver of good things. Rightly, then, have you been likened to those serpents whose ears are stopped against the charmers. "For their wrath," says the Scripture, "is after the likeness of the serpent, like the deaf asp that stops her ears, which will not hear the voice of the charmers." But do you be charmed out of your savagery, and receive the gentle and our Word, and spit out the deadly venom, that it may be granted you, as fully as may be, to put off corruption, as those serpents put off age. Hear me, and do not stop your ears nor block your hearing, but lay to mind the things said. Fair is the medicine of immortality; at last stay your creeping coils. "For the enemies of the Lord shall lick the dust," it says. Lift up your faces from the earth into the upper air; look up to heaven; marvel; cease lying in wait for the heel of the just and hindering the way of truth; become prudent and harmless; perhaps the Lord will grant you the wing of simplicity — for he has chosen to give wings to the earth-born — that, leaving the clefts, you may dwell in the heavens. Only let us repent with the whole heart, that with the whole heart we may be able to contain God. "Hope in him," it says, "all the congregation of the people; pour out before him all your hearts." He speaks to those emptied of wickedness: he pities and fills them with righteousness. Believe, O man, in the man and God; believe, O man, in him who suffered and is worshipped. Believe, you slaves, in the living God who was dead; all men, believe in the only God of all men; believe, and receive as your wage salvation. Seek out God, "and your soul shall live." He who seeks out God is busy about his own salvation; you have found God, you have life. Let us seek, then, that we may also live. The wage of finding is life with God. "Let all that seek you be glad and rejoice in you, and let them say continually, God be magnified." A fair hymn of God is an immortal man, built up in righteousness, in whom the oracles of the truth are engraved. For where else than in a sober soul should righteousness be inscribed? Where love? Where modesty? Where gentleness? Those who have sealed up these divine Scriptures upon the soul ought, I think, to count wisdom a fair starting-place for those who turn to whatever part of life, and to reckon this same wisdom a waveless harbour of salvation; through which the fathers of children are good, those who have run to the Father; and good are the sons to their parents, who have understood the Son; and good are the husbands of wives, who remember the Bridegroom; and good are the masters of servants, who have been redeemed from the uttermost slavery. O happier than the wandering among men are the beasts! They feed upon their ignorance, as you do, but they do not counterfeit the truth; there is among them no race of flatterers; fishes are not superstitious; birds do not commit idolatry; they are astonished at the one heaven alone, since they cannot understand God, having been deemed unworthy of the Word. Then are you not ashamed, having made yourselves more irrational than the irrational, who through so many ages have worn yourselves out in godlessness? You have become children, then youths, then striplings, then men, but never good. At least respect old age, and, being at the setting of life, be sober; and even at the end of life recognize God, that the end of life may take up for you a beginning of salvation. Grow old toward superstition; come young toward piety. God will reckon you guileless children. Let the Athenian, then, follow the laws of Solon, and the Argive those of Phoroneus, and the Spartan those of Lycurgus; but if you enroll yourself as God's, heaven is your fatherland and God your lawgiver. And what are the laws? "You shall not kill; you shall not commit adultery; you shall not corrupt boys; you shall not steal; you shall not bear false witness; you shall love the Lord your God." And there are the complements of these, rational laws and holy words inscribed in the very hearts: "You shall love your neighbour as yourself; and to him that smites you on the cheek offer also the other; and you shall not covet, for by lust alone you have committed adultery." How much better, then, for men than to obtain their lusts, not even at the beginning to wish to lust after what they ought not. But you cannot endure the austerity of salvation; rather, just as we are pleased with the sweet among foods, preferring them for the smoothness of the pleasure, while the bitter, which roughen the sense, heal and make us whole — for the austerity of medicines strengthens those weak in the stomach — so custom delights and tickles, but the one, custom, thrusts into the pit; the other, truth, leads up to heaven, rough indeed at first, but a good nurse of youth. And august is this women's quarter, and sober the council of elders; nor is she hard of access, nor impossible to attain, but she is the nearest indweller of us, as Moses the all-wise hints, dwelling in the three parts that are ours — hands and mouth and heart — a genuine symbol that the truth is fulfilled by all three, by counsel and deed and word. And do not fear this either, lest the many and delightful things imagined take you away from wisdom; of your own free will you will pass over the trifling of custom, just as children too, when they have become men, cast away their playthings. With unsurpassable speed and easily-approached goodwill the divine power, shining upon the earth, has filled the whole with the seed of salvation. For not in so short a time would the Lord have accomplished so great a work without divine care — despised in appearance, worshipped in deed, the purifier and saviour and gentle one, the divine Word, the most manifest, truly God, made equal to the Master of all, because he was his Son, and the Word was in God; neither, when he was first proclaimed beforehand, disbelieved, nor, when he had taken upon him the mask of man and moulded himself in flesh and played out the saving drama of humanity, unknown; for he was a genuine champion and fellow-contestant of the creature, and, swiftly distributed among all men, having risen faster than the sun from the Father's very will, with the greatest ease shone upon us God, presenting both whence he was and who he was by the things he taught and showed — the Word, the bearer of the truce and the reconciler and our Saviour, the life-giving fountain, peaceful, poured out over the whole face of the earth, through whom, so to speak, all things have now become a sea of good things.

Consider a little, if you will, from above, the divine benefit. The first man played, free, in paradise, for he was a child of God; but when, yielding to pleasure (the serpent is the allegory of pleasure, creeping upon its belly, an earthly wickedness, fed upon matter), he was led aside by lusts, the child, made manly by disobedience and disobeying his Father, was ashamed before God. See what pleasure availed: the man who through simplicity was free was found bound by sins. The Lord wished to loose him again from his bonds, and, bound in flesh (this is a divine mystery), he subdued the serpent and enslaved the tyrant, death; and — most marvellous of all — that man who had been led astray by pleasure, bound by corruption, he showed loosed by hands stretched out. O mystic wonder! The Lord was laid low, but man rose up; and he that fell from paradise receives a greater prize for his obedience — the heavens. Wherefore it seems to me that, since the Word himself has come to us from heaven, we ought no longer to go to human teaching, busying ourselves about Athens and the rest of Greece, and Ionia besides. For if our teacher is he who has filled all things with holy powers — by creation, salvation, beneficence, lawgiving, prophecy, teaching — the teacher now instructs us in all things, and the whole has already become Athens and Greece through the Word. For surely you did not believe a poetic myth that records Minos the Cretan as the familiar of Zeus, and yet will disbelieve us, who have become disciples of God, having taken up the truly true wisdom, which the topmost of the philosophers only hinted at, but the disciples of Christ both grasped and proclaimed. And indeed all Christ, so to speak, is not divided: he is neither barbarian nor Jew nor Greek, neither male nor female, but a new man, remade by the Holy Spirit of God.

Then the other counsels and precepts are paltry and concern particulars: whether one ought to marry, whether to take part in public life, whether to beget children; but the only universal exhortation, and that for the whole of life, in every season, in every circumstance, straining toward the chief end, life, is piety; in accordance with which alone it is necessary to live, that we may live forever. Philosophy, as the elders say, is a long-lasting counsel, wooing the eternal love of wisdom; but "the commandment of the Lord is far-shining, enlightening the eyes." Receive Christ, receive sight, receive your light, "that you may know well both God and man." "Lovely is the Word that enlightened us," beyond gold and precious stone; "it is sweet beyond honey and the honeycomb." For how is he not lovely who made the mind, buried in darkness, clear, and sharpened the light-bringing eyes of the soul? For just as, the sun not being, for all the other stars it would be night over all, so, had we not known the Word and been illumined by him, we should have differed in nothing from fattened birds, fed in darkness and nourished for death. Let us receive the light, that we may receive God; let us receive the light, and become disciples of the Lord. For this very thing has been promised to the Father: "I will declare your name to my brethren; in the midst of the assembly I will hymn you." Hymn and declare to me your Father, God; your tales shall save, your song shall instruct me. Until now I wandered, seeking God; but since you light my way, Lord, I both find God through you and receive the Father from you; I become your fellow-heir, since you were not ashamed of me as a brother. Let us put away, then, let us put away forgetfulness of the truth; the ignorance and the darkness that stands in our way, like a mist upon the sight, having put it down, let us behold the God who truly is, first hymning to him this voice: "Hail, light." Light from heaven shone upon us, who were buried in darkness and shut up in the shadow of death, purer than the sun, sweeter than the life here. That light is eternal life, and whatever has partaken of it lives; but night fears the light, and, setting through fear, gives way to the day of the Lord; all things have become unsleeping light, and the setting has turned to a rising. This is what the new creation desired; for he who rides upon all things, the sun of righteousness, goes round upon mankind impartially, imitating the Father, who makes his sun rise upon all men and sheds down the dew of truth. He has turned the setting into a rising, and crucified death into life, and, snatching man out of destruction, has hung him up in the ether, transplanting corruption into incorruption and changing earth into heavens — the husbandman of God, "signalling good things, and rousing the peoples to a good work," reminding them of the true livelihood, and granting us the great and truly divine and inalienable inheritance of the Father, making man divine by heavenly teaching, "putting laws into their understanding and writing them upon the heart." What laws does he prescribe? "That all shall know God, from small to great"; and "I will be merciful to them," says God, "and their sins I will remember no more." Let us receive the laws of life; let us be persuaded by God exhorting; let us learn of him, that he may be merciful; let us render, even to him who has no need, a thankful wage of well-being, as a kind of rent to God for our dwelling here. "Gold for bronze, a hundred oxen's worth for nine." For a little faith he gives you so great an earth to till, water to drink and other to sail, air to breathe, fire to serve you, a world to dwell in; from here he has granted you to send out a colony to the heavens. These great and so many works and graces he has let out to you for a little faith. Then those who have believed the cheats accept their amulets and incantations as supposedly saving; but you will not bind upon yourselves the heavenly amulet itself, the saving Word, and, trusting the incantation of God, be released from the passions, which are diseases of the soul, and torn away from sin? For sin is eternal death. Are you utterly toothless and blind, like moles, doing nothing but eating and living in darkness, dribbling away in corruption? But there is — there is — the truth that cried out, "Out of darkness light shall shine." Let the light, then, shine in the hidden part of the man, in the heart, and let the rays of knowledge rise, revealing and making to shine the man hidden within, the disciple of the light, the friend and fellow-heir of Christ — especially when the most precious and most reverend name of a good Father comes to the knowledge of a pious and good child of a good Father, who commands gentle things and enjoins on the child the things that save. He who obeys him has the advantage in every way: he follows God, he obeys the Father, he came to know him through wandering, he loved God, he loved his neighbour, he fulfilled the commandment, he seeks the prize, he demands the promise. And it is ever set before God to save the flock of men. For this cause too the good God sent the good shepherd. And the Word, having unfolded the truth, showed men the height of salvation, that, repenting, they might be saved, or, disobeying, be judged. This is the proclamation of righteousness, good tidings to those who obey, judgement to those who disobey. But while the loud-clamouring trumpet, sounding, gathers soldiers and proclaims war, shall not Christ, having breathed a peaceful strain to the ends of the earth, gather his own peaceful soldiers? He has gathered, O man, the bloodless army by blood and by the Word, and has put into their hands the kingdom of the heavens. The trumpet of Christ is his gospel: he sounded it, and we heard. Let us arm ourselves peacefully, putting on the breastplate of righteousness and taking up the shield of faith and setting about our head the helmet of salvation, and let us sharpen the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God.
