So the apostle peacefully draws us up in array; these are our invulnerable weapons; with these armed, let us set ourselves against the wicked one; the fiery darts of the wicked one let us quench with the watery points dipped by the Word, requiting kindnesses with thankful blessings and honouring God with the divine Word. "For while you are yet speaking," it says, "he will say, Behold, I am here." O this holy and blessed power, through which God lives as a fellow-citizen with men! Better, then, and best, to become at once the imitator and the servant of the best of beings; for no one can imitate God except by serving him in holiness, nor again serve and reverence him except by imitating him. The heavenly and truly divine love thus comes to men, whenever in the very soul the truly fair, kindled by the divine Word, can shine forth; and, what is greatest, salvation runs side by side with the genuine willing to be saved, choice and life being yoked together, so to speak. Therefore this exhortation of truth alone, like the most faithful of friends, abides with us to the last breath, and becomes a good escort, with the whole and perfect breath of the soul, to those who depart toward heaven. Why, then, do I exhort you? I am eager that you be saved. This Christ wills; in one word he gives you life. And who is he? Learn briefly. The Word of truth, the Word of incorruption, who regenerates man, bringing him back to the truth, the goad of salvation, who drives out corruption, who chases away death, who has built up in men a temple, that in men he may set up God. Purify the temple, and the pleasures and the slacknesses, like a flower of a day, leave to the wind and the fire; the fruits of self-control cultivate prudently, and set yourself up as firstfruits to God, that you may be not only his work but also his grace; and both befit the friend of Christ, both to appear worthy of the kingdom and to be deemed worthy of the kingdom.

Let us flee, then, custom; let us flee it like a dangerous headland, or the menace of Charybdis, or the fabled Sirens. It chokes man, turns him away from the truth, leads him from life; it is a snare, a pit, a hole, a greedy evil — custom. "Keep your ship away from that smoke and wave." Let us flee, fellow-voyagers, let us flee this wave; it belches fire; it is a wicked island, heaped with bones and corpses, and there sings within it a fair little harlot, pleasure, delighting in vulgar music: "Come hither, much-praised Odysseus, great glory of the Achaeans; bring your ship to land, that you may hear a more divine voice." She praises you, O sailor, and calls you much-hymned, and the harlot makes the glory of the Greeks her own. Let her feed upon the dead; a heavenly breath helps you. Pass pleasure by; she beguiles. "Let no woman, with her decked-out rear, deceive your mind, prattling coaxing words, prying into your barn." Sail past the song; it works death. Only if you will, you have conquered destruction, and, bound fast to the wood, you shall be loosed from all corruption; the Word of God shall steer you, and the Holy Spirit shall bring you to anchor in the harbours of the heavens. Then you shall behold my God, and be initiated into those holy mysteries, and enjoy the things hidden in the heavens, reserved for me, "which neither ear has heard nor has entered into the heart of any."

"And truly I seem to see two suns and a double Thebes," said one as he revelled to the idols, drunk with unmingled ignorance; but I would pity him in his drunken folly, and would call him who is thus beside himself to a sober salvation, since the Lord too welcomes the repentance, and not the death, of the sinner. Come, O madman, not leaning on the thyrsus, not wreathed with ivy; cast off the headband, cast off the fawn-skin, be sober; I will show you the Word and the mysteries of the Word, recounting them according to your own image. This is a mountain beloved of God, not laid out for tragedies like Cithaeron, but dedicated to the dramas of truth, a sober mountain, shaded with pure groves. And in it revel not the sisters of thunder-struck Semele, the Maenads, who are initiated into a foul distribution of flesh, but the daughters of God, the fair lambs, declaring the august rites of the Word, gathering a sober chorus. The chorus are the just; the song is a hymn of the King of all; the maidens make music, the angels glorify, the prophets speak, a sound of music is sent forth; at a run they pursue the holy band; those who are called hasten, longing to receive the Father. Come to me too, old man — yes, you — leaving Thebes, and casting away your divination and your Bacchic frenzy, be led by the hand to the truth. Behold, I give you the wood to lean upon; hasten, Teiresias, believe; you shall see. Christ shines more brightly than the sun, through whom the eyes of the blind see again; night shall flee from you, fire shall be afraid, death shall depart; you shall see the heavens, O old man, you who do not see Thebes. O the truly holy mysteries! O the pure light! I am led with torches to behold the heavens and God; I become holy as I am initiated; the Lord is hierophant, and seals the initiate as he leads him to the light, and presents to the Father him who has believed, to be kept through the ages. These are the revels of my mysteries. If you will, be initiated too, and you shall dance with angels about the unbegotten and imperishable and only truly existing God, the Word of God hymning together with us. This Jesus is eternal, one great High Priest of the one God who is at once the same and the Father; he prays for men and exhorts men: "Hearken, you countless tribes" — or rather, all you of men that are rational, both barbarians and Greeks; the whole race of men I call, of whom I am the Maker by the will of the Father. Come to me, to be marshalled under one God and the one Word of God; and do not only excel the irrational animals by reason, but, alone of all mortal things, take from me the harvest of immortality. For I will, I will impart to you this grace too, supplying the whole benefit, incorruption; and I give you the Word as a gift, the knowledge of God; I give you myself, perfect. For this is what I am; this is what God wills; this is symphony, this is the harmony of the Father; this is the Son, this is Christ, this is the Word of God, the arm of the Lord, the power of all things, the will of the Father. O you who were of old images, but not all of them like — I wish to set you right toward the archetype, that you may become like to me also. I will anoint you with the unguent of faith, through which you cast off corruption, and I will show bare the figure of righteousness, through which you ascend to God. "Come unto me, all you that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest; take my yoke upon you, and learn of me, for I am gentle and lowly of heart, and you shall find rest unto your souls; for my yoke is good and my burden is light." Let us hasten, let us run, O statues of the Word, dear to God and like to God; let us hasten, let us run, let us take up his yoke, let us put on incorruption, let us love Christ, the fair charioteer of men; he led the colt under the yoke together with the old beast, and, having harnessed the pair of mankind, he steers the chariot straight toward immortality, hastening to God, to fulfil clearly what he hinted at — first into Jerusalem, but now driving into the heavens, a fairest spectacle to the Father, the eternal, victorious Son. Let us, then, become emulous of fair things and lovers of God, and let us gain the greatest of goods, God and life. Our helper is the Word; let us take courage in him, and let no such longing for silver and gold, nor for glory, ever come upon us, as the longing for the very Word of truth. For neither is it pleasing to God himself, if we count the things of greatest worth as least, and choose rather the manifest outrages of ignorance and unlearning and idleness and idolatry, and the uttermost impiety. For not without reason do the children of the philosophers reckon all that the senseless do to be acts of unholiness and impiety; and, describing ignorance itself as a form of madness, they confess that the many are nothing else than mad. There is no room, then, to doubt, or to be mad; but, holding fast to the truth with all our strength, we must follow God with all our power, being sober, and reckoning all things to be his, as indeed they are; and besides, having learned that we are his fairest possession, we must entrust ourselves to God, loving the Lord God, and reckoning this our work throughout the whole of life. And if the things of friends are common, and man is dear to God — for indeed he is a friend of God, the Word mediating — then all things become man's, because all things are God's, and all things are common to the two friends, God and man. It is time, then, for us to say that the pious man alone is rich and sober and well-born, and in this respect an image of God with the likeness, and to declare and believe that, having become just and holy with prudence through Christ Jesus, he is to this extent already like even to God. For the prophet does not conceal the grace, saying: "I said, You are gods, and all of you sons of the Most High." For us, us he has adopted, and of us alone he wishes to be called Father, not of the disobedient. For thus indeed stand our affairs, who are the followers of Christ: as the counsels, such also the words; as the words, such the deeds; and as the works, such the life. Good throughout is the whole life of men who have come to know Christ. Enough, I think, of words, though out of love toward man I have gone on rather far, pouring out what I had from God, as one exhorting toward the greatest of goods, salvation. For concerning the life that has no pause at all, not even the words are willing ever to cease their hierophany. And for you there is left this final end, the profitable, to choose — either judgement or grace; for I, for my part, deem it not even worthy of doubt which of the two is better, nor is it lawful to compare life with destruction.
